sense: a reason given to explain a fault

evidence: Cic. Att. 12.29.1: quaerenda erit excūsātiō ad Brūtum
terms.comment: Often with a genitive of the ground pleaded, excūsātiō aetātis, valētūdinis, the excuse of age, of health (Lewis & Short). Excūsātiōnem accipere, to accept an excuse.

terms.gloss: excuse; make (someone’s) excuses; plead as an excuse
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; aliquem alicui, mē (tibi) excūsō
evidence: Cic. Att. 15.28: Atticae meae velim mē ita excūsēs ut omnem culpam in tē trānsferās
Cic. Q. Fr. 2.2.1 (Lewis & Short): prīmum mē tibi excūsō in eō ipsō, in quō tē accūsō
terms.comment: To clear of blame, the opposite of accūsāre: mē tibi excūsō, I apologise (see I apologise); ut excūser morbī causā, that I be excused on grounds of illness (Cic. Att. 12.13.2). For “excuse me” and forgiving a fault, see excuse me, forgive.

evidence: Ter. Eun. 138: fingit causās nē det sēdulō
terms.comment: The general word for a cause or reason; it is also a feigned reason, a pretext: causās fingere, to make up excuses; per causam, on the pretext of (Lewis & Short). Its everyday senses are a reason and a lawsuit (see reason).

phrases.latin: Atticae meae velim mē ita excūsēs ut omnem culpam in tē trānsferās
phrases.english: please make my excuses to my little Attica, and put all the blame on yourself

phrases.latin: postquam sēnsit mē tēcum quoque rem habēre, fingit causās nē det sēdulō.
phrases.english: once he realised I was seeing you too, he kept making up excuses not to hand her over.

phrases.latin: sed in hōc homine nūllam accipiō excūsātiōnem.
phrases.english: But in this man’s case I accept no excuse.

sources: Lewis & Short: excusatio · Lewis & Short: excuso · Lewis & Short: causa
